transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-09-14
- Time: 09:00 PT / 16:00 UTC
- Duration: ~52 minutes
- Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE); Priya Nair (Redwood SE); Dana Ortiz (CTO, Thalassa Labs); Marco Liu (SRE); Erin Park (Head of Security); Sofia Gomez (Networking)

Summary:
Thalassa Labs is evaluating Redwood for Private onramp into their VPCs across EU and US regions. Main constraints: strict egress IP allowlist, some regions locked to EU-only data processing, preference for private endpoints over internet egress, and wanting predictable latency for low-latency inference. They are comparing Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private on cost/latency and need SOC2/KMS assurances. Next steps: share peering diagram options, KMS integration notes, and schedule a hands-on network workshop.

Topics covered:
- VPC peering vs PrivateLink-like endpoints
- Regional constraints and data residency (EU-only workloads)
- Egress allowlist and IP churn considerations
- Latency SLOs and dedicated capacity vs hosted fallbacks
- KMS/HSM key access patterns and audit logs
- Rollout plan and timeline for a POC

Action items (captured in metadata above)

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro - I'm Alex, account lead, and Priya is our solutions engineer. How are you all?
[00:10] Dana (Thalassa): Hi, Dana here, thanks. We want to dig into networking — private onramp, regions, egress constraints.
[00:18] Alex (Redwood): Great. Could you lay out current infra and what "private onramp" means for you?
[00:25] Marco (Thalassa): Sure. We're mostly k8s on AWS, multiple VPCs — US-west, us-east and eu-west. We have strict egress allowlists: only certain IPs can talk out. Some workloads must stay EU-only due to contracts. Ideally we want Redwood Private deployed into our VPC or a peered VPC with private endpoints, no public internet egress.
[00:45] Priya (Redwood): That makes sense. We support a couple patterns: VPC peering/transit gateway style routing to Dedicated/Private nodes, and private endpoint (like PrivateLink) for the control plane and data plane. Both can avoid public internet. For tight allowlists we can provide static egress IP ranges for Private or Dedicated, but Hosted has more variable IPs.
[01:10] Erin (Thalassa): How static are those egress IPs? Our security team will only allow CIDRs that don't change frequently.
[01:18] Priya (Redwood): For Redwood Private (customer-managed VPC) you control the egress, so that's static by design. With Redwood Dedicated we can reserve capacity in a peered VPC and provide an egress block that changes only with planned maintenance; still, we publish a small range. Hosted API is the one with ephemeral IPs and we don't recommend that for allowlist-only environments.
[01:42] Dana (Thalassa): So Dedicated could be okay if the IPs are stable. But what about latency? Some of our user-facing inference needs <50ms p99.
[01:53] Priya (Redwood): Latency depends on model size and instance type. Dedicated with pinned GPU pools in-region gives predictable p99s; Private in your VPC eliminates network hop to the public internet so that's optimal. There's tradeoff: Private usually costs more operationally on your side, Dedicated is a middle ground. We can share benchmarks.
[02:12] Alex (Redwood): Also worth noting automatic fallback routes — if a region is saturated we can route to a compatible model variant in another region but with a higher cost/latency. We'll surface that in the routing policy.
[02:26] Sofia (Thalassa): For EU-only workloads then that fallback isn't acceptable unless it's also EU. Can we pin region constraints?
[02:35] Priya (Redwood): Yes, region-level routing constraints are supported. You can set strict region gating so no requests for certain projects leave eu-west. There is also the option to deploy Private control planes in-region for more isolation.
[02:50] Marco (Thalassa): On peering: we use a transit gateway between many VPCs. Would Redwood need a new peering per VPC or can we integrate via the transit?
[02:59] Priya (Redwood): We can peer to a central VPC attached to the transit gateway, so you don't need N peering sessions. We'll ask for a diagram of your transit setup; Priya will send an example.
[03:13] Erin (Thalassa): KMS — we require customer-managed keys for any PII inference. How does Redwood handle KMS/HSM integrations?
[03:21] Priya (Redwood): Redwood Private supports BYOK via AWS KMS aliases or HSM connectors. All audit logs are exported to your CloudWatch/Splunk. For Dedicated we have options to integrate with your KMS using cross-account grants. We'll share the SOC2 + KMS section from our security pack.
[03:39] Dana (Thalassa): Any compliance gap? We need ISO27001 and SOC2 Type II.
[03:45] Alex (Redwood): Redwood is SOC2 Type II, and we can provide our ISO attestation where available; for Private deployments some responsibilities shift to the customer but we provide the artifacts you'd need for audits.
[03:57] Marco (Thalassa): About IP planning — egress bandwidth can spike during batch jobs. Do you support burst capacity?
[04:06] Priya (Redwood): Yes, Dedicated can be configured with burst capacity and autoscaling. On Private, since it's in your network, you can scale the node pool; we recommend configuring flow logs and setting rate limits at the subnet level if you have tight egress windows.
[04:24] Dana (Thalassa): Are there constraints around PrivateLink-style endpoints? We have limits on number of endpoints and cross-account endpoints cause extra costs.
[04:33] Priya (Redwood): Good point. We usually propose two patterns: 1) PrivateLink endpoints into a Redwood-managed VPC that you peer to, or 2) host Redwood nodes directly in your VPC (we provide an image/helm chart). PrivateLink reduces blast radius but costs more per endpoint; hosting in your VPC gives you full control and simpler egress. We'll sketch both.
[04:54] Alex (Redwood): Also, we can support split-control: control plane in Redwood hosted (with a private control-plane tunnel) while inference nodes live in your VPC, so the control plane talks over a TLS tunnel and doesn't carry data payloads. That reduces ops surface.
[05:09] Sofia (Thalassa): For EU, we want all inference nodes in eu-west; control plane can be elsewhere as long as logs/audits are kept in EU. Is that possible?
[05:18] Priya (Redwood): We can keep audit logs and telemetry exported to your EU tenant. Control plane metadata might still hit our control plane if you use hosted control; but Private can remove that. We'll document the tradeoffs.
[05:31] Marco (Thalassa): Pricing — can you give a rough delta between Dedicated and Private?
[05:36] Alex (Redwood): Ballpark: Dedicated is lower upfront operational complexity and we manage the infra; Private shifts more operational responsibility to you and may have licensing or platform fees. We'll send a tailored sheet after we see your usage profile.
[05:47] Dana (Thalassa): What's the usual POC timeline? Our compliance window is tight; we'd like to move in 6 weeks if feasible.
[05:55] Priya (Redwood): A small POC with a single VPC + sample model can be 2-4 weeks for networking + onboarding, longer if we need custom KMS/HSM integration. 6 weeks is achievable if we run parallel tasks.
[06:07] Erin (Thalassa): Are there any customer references for similar setups — transit gateway + private endpoints + EU gating?
[06:13] Alex (Redwood): We can provide anonymized references and a short case study of a fintech customer we onboarded with similar constraints. I'll drop that.
[06:21] Marco (Thalassa): One more thing: do you support per-route token-level cost breakouts? Our finance team wants chargeback data.
[06:28] Priya (Redwood): Yes, Redwood Console gives token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route/model. For Private deployments we can export usage metrics to your billing stack.
[06:38] Alex (Redwood): Ok let's talk specifics — Sofia, can you describe the VPC CIDRs and transit layout quickly?
[06:44] Sofia (Thalassa): US-west: 10.10.0.0/16, us-east: 10.20.0.0/16, eu-west: 10.30.0.0/16. Transit gateway connects all. We have an on-prem datacenter peered via VPN to the transit too.
[06:58] Priya (Redwood): Perfect. We'll propose a central Redwood peered VPC or an in-VPC node group. For the latter we need subnet level access and an EIP plan if any external egress required.
[07:10] Dana (Thalassa): If we run nodes in-VPC, who handles patching and runtime updates?
[07:16] Priya (Redwood): We provide a managed agent and upgrade tool; ops can decide whether Redwood pushes updates or if you approve them. It's configurable.
[07:26] Marco (Thalassa): Network ACLs — our infra team uses very strict NACLs. Will that block health checks?
[07:33] Priya (Redwood): We'll provide a minimal port list. Most traffic is TLS on standard ports, but we do use ephemeral ports for gRPC health checks in some setups; can work with explicit rules.
[07:44] Alex (Redwood): Do you have any questions about fallback and graceful degradation we should highlight?
[07:49] Erin (Thalassa): Yes — if eu-west saturates, we need clear behavior: queue, reject, or route within EU only.
[07:56] Priya (Redwood): You can configure SLOs and fallback policies per route: strict (reject if can't fulfill in region), tolerant (route to nearest compatible EU region), or best-effort (route globally). We'll note that in the design.
[08:10] Dana (Thalassa): Ok good. Anything around quotas or rate limits?
[08:15] Alex (Redwood): We enforce token and rps quotas; with Dedicated/Private you can set higher thresholds and control per-token billing.
[08:22] Sofia (Thalassa): A non-network question — do you support model quantization or lower-cost variants that might reduce egress/bandwidth by reducing payload sizes?
[08:31] Priya (Redwood): Model quantization reduces GPU memory and latency; payload size is mostly prompt + response text. We do have options for streaming vs chunked responses to help bandwidth costs. We'll include suggestions.
[08:44] Marco (Thalassa): Any gotchas with cross-account peering and lambda egress? We use cross-account lambdas in us-east that invoke services in eu-west through the transit.
[08:55] Priya (Redwood): That's fine; we'll need the ARN and IAM permissions for cross-account peering and recommend using VPC endpoints for the functions. We'll document the permission set.
[09:06] Alex (Redwood): Let's recap next steps: 1) Priya to draw two designs — in-VPC node group and PrivateLink peering into a Redwood VPC; 2) Alex to send pricing delta and SOC2/KMS docs; 3) Thalassa to send CIDRs, egress IPs, and any compliance timelines.
[09:23] Dana (Thalassa): Sounds good. We'll try to get the CIDR list today.
[09:27] Alex (Redwood): Great. Any other questions?
[09:30] Erin (Thalassa): One last item — how do you handle KV cache persistence across restarts? We rely on warm cache for latency.
[09:38] Priya (Redwood): Our runtime supports persistent KV cache snapshots; on Private in-VPC we can persist to local SSDs or S3 per your preference. We'll also provide best practices for cache pinning to reduce cold-start tail.
[09:53] Marco (Thalassa): Excellent. If we do a POC, what's the minimum footprint?
[09:58] Priya (Redwood): A single 8-GPU node pool with a small routing front is enough for a functional POC. For low-latency needs we might bump to faster GPUs.
[10:08] Alex (Redwood): That wraps the core. We'll follow up with the diagram and docs. Thanks everyone.
